cards.prompt: Which English king sealed Magna Carta?
cards.funFactWhy: Pope Innocent III annulled the 1215 charter just ten weeks after Runnymede, sparking a civil war before nine-year-old Henry III reissued it.
cards.helpfulHint: He was the unpopular younger brother of Richard the Lionheart and the classic royal villain of Robin Hood legends.

cards.prompt: Which empire built Machu Picchu?
cards.funFactWhy: Raised in the mid-1400s under Emperor Pachacuti without mortar or iron tools, its dry-stone blocks lock together so tightly that earthquakes merely make them dance back into place.
cards.helpfulHint: Its emperors ruled the Andes from Cusco and kept accounts on knotted cords called quipu.

cards.prompt: In 1932, the Australian army deployed machine guns against a surprisingly agile opponent that still won the campaign. What bird outsmarted them?
cards.funFactWhy: Soldiers burned through thousands of rounds in Western Australia yet barely dented the 20,000-bird flock, leading Major Meredith to liken them to tanks that could split into disciplined squads.
cards.helpfulHint: This tall, flightless native shares Australia's coat of arms with the kangaroo because neither creature walks backward easily.

cards.prompt: In 1788, Habsburg soldiers reportedly mistook their own multilingual comrades for Ottoman raiders after a schnapps brawl, sparking a chaotic nighttime rout named for what town?
cards.funFactWhy: Historians suspect later storytellers inflated the casualty toll, yet Emperor Joseph II really did tumble off his horse into a creek during the panic.
cards.helpfulHint: Situated in western Romania's Banat region along the Timis River, this Habsburg camp lay right in the path of the advancing Ottoman vanguard.

cards.prompt: During his lavish 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca, which West African monarch distributed so much gold in Cairo that it crashed Egyptian bullion prices for over a decade?
cards.funFactWhy: On his journey home from Mecca, he deliberately borrowed gold back from Cairo moneylenders at steep interest just to absorb the surplus he had accidentally unleashed.
cards.helpfulHint: The 1375 Catalan Atlas portrays this Mali Empire ruler enthroned with a golden orb in his outstretched hand.

cards.prompt: Which 1648 pair of treaties negotiated simultaneously in Munster and Osnabruck ended the Thirty Years' War and codified modern state sovereignty?
cards.funFactWhy: Catholic envoys met in Munster while Protestant delegates bargained 50 kilometers away in Osnabruck so rival diplomats never had to dine under the same roof.
cards.helpfulHint: Political scientists still name the international order of sovereign territorial states after this northwestern German region.

cards.prompt: Link each civilization-shaping breakthrough to the historic culture that pioneered it.
cards.funFactWhy: Han court official Cai Lun standardized pulp papermaking around 105 CE using mulberry bark, hemp waste, old rags, and worn fishing nets.
cards.helpfulHint: Wedge-shaped clay tablets belong to Mesopotamia, while Johannes Gutenberg's workshop sat in Mainz along the Rhine.

match4.instruction: Match each breakthrough to its originating civilization or era

cards.prompt: Pair each landmark peace treaty with the conflict it formally brought to a close.
cards.funFactWhy: Brokering the 1905 talks at a New Hampshire naval shipyard made Theodore Roosevelt the first sitting U.S. president to win the Nobel Peace Prize.
cards.helpfulHint: Use the treaty dates as compass points: 1783 recognized American independence, and 1905 mediated a clash in East Asia.

match4.instruction: Match each treaty to the war it ended

cards.prompt: Match four Wonders of the Ancient World to the historic port or city where travelers once marveled at them.
cards.funFactWhy: Persian satrap Mausolus built such an extravagant tomb in Caria that his own name became the everyday English word for any monumental burial chamber.
cards.helpfulHint: Ptolemaic Egypt guarded its Nile Delta harbor with a towering beacon, while a bronze sun god watched over an Aegean island.

match4.instruction: Match each Ancient Wonder to its historic home

cards.prompt: Arrange these four seismic turning points in world history from earliest to latest.
cards.funFactWhy: Just 200 years separated Parisians toppling the Bastille from Berliners chiseling apart the Cold War concrete wall.
cards.helpfulHint: Ottoman cannons breached Byzantine walls centuries before the French Revolution, and powered flight arrived right after 1900.

cards.prompt: Order these four ancient legal and political watersheds from earliest to latest.
cards.funFactWhy: Babylon's black basalt stele preceded the Roman Republic by more than a millennium and still sits on display at the Louvre.
cards.helpfulHint: Babylonian law came first, Rome's Republic began centuries before the Ides of March, and Constantine legalized Christianity in the fourth century CE.

cards.prompt: Line up these four modern unification and independence milestones from earliest to latest.
cards.funFactWhy: When the Gold Coast became Ghana in 1957 under Kwame Nkrumah, it kicked off a wave that saw over thirty African nations gain independence within a decade.
cards.helpfulHint: Italy unified during the 19th century, South Asia won independence right after World War II, and the Cold War ended last.

initialOrder.label: Proclamation of the Kingdom of Italy

cards.prompt: Tap ALL THREE English monarchs who reigned as members of the House of Tudor.
cards.funFactWhy: All three children of Henry VIII eventually wore the crown, yet none left a biological heir, handing England to the Scottish Stuarts in 1603.
cards.helpfulHint: Think of the six-wife father and his two famous daughters who ruled in the 1500s.

cards.prompt: Three of these pre-1500 powers flourished in the Americas. Spot the ONE imposter that ruled on another continent.
cards.funFactWhy: Centered along the Niger River bend at Gao and Timbuktu, the West African outlier grew into one of the largest states in African history.
cards.helpfulHint: One of these four empires controlled trans-Saharan trade routes and Timbuktu rather than Mesoamerica or the Andes.

cards.prompt: Tap ALL THREE historic luminaries who were alive on New Year's Day of the year 1500.
cards.funFactWhy: In 1500, a 25-year-old sculptor had just finished the Pieta, a 48-year-old polymath was leaving Milan, and a 27-year-old astronomer was lecturing in Rome.
cards.helpfulHint: The German printing pioneer died in 1468, while both the Bard of Avon and Pisa's telescope icon were born in 1564.

cards.prompt: Dial in the year RMS Titanic struck an iceberg and sank on its maiden North Atlantic crossing.
cards.funFactWhy: Two years before World War I erupted, the tragedy led maritime nations to create the International Ice Patrol and require enough lifeboats for every soul aboard.
cards.helpfulHint: It happened in April right between the turn of the 20th century and the outbreak of World War I.

cards.prompt: Zero in on the year French soldiers rebuilding a Nile Delta fort unearthed the Rosetta Stone.
cards.funFactWhy: Because its decree appeared in hieroglyphs, Demotic, and Ancient Greek, linguist Jean-Francois Champollion finally unlocked Egyptian hieroglyphs 23 years later.
cards.helpfulHint: It was uncovered during Napoleon Bonaparte's Egyptian expedition right at the close of the 18th century.

cards.prompt: The 1896 Anglo-Zanzibar War holds the Guinness record as history's shortest war. Dial in how many minutes it lasted.
cards.funFactWhy: Royal Navy cruisers began shelling the sultan's palace at 9:02 AM, and the flag came down in surrender before most Londoners had finished their morning tea.
cards.helpfulHint: It finished well under an hour — shorter than a single half of a regulation soccer match.

cards.prompt: Identify this history-making monarch as the clues grow sharper.
cards.funFactWhy: She lived closer in time to the 1969 Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid of Giza around 2560 BCE.
cards.helpfulHint: She was the last active pharaoh of Hellenistic Egypt before Rome annexed the realm.

clues: Though crowned in Egypt, she was the first sovereign of her Macedonian Greek dynasty to bother learning the Egyptian language.
Plutarch recounts that she smuggled herself past palace guards bundled inside a linen sack to win an audience with Julius Caesar.
She later allied with Mark Antony against Octavian, ending the Ptolemaic dynasty after the naval Battle of Actium.

cards.prompt: Name this celebrated medieval globetrotter from three escalating clues.
cards.funFactWhy: On his deathbed in 1324, friends urged him to retract his tall tales of paper money and burning black rocks, to which he supposedly replied he had not told half of what he saw.
cards.helpfulHint: Every swimming-pool game of blind tag echoes the first and last name of this Venetian merchant.

clues: He dictated his blockbuster travelogue to a romance novelist named Rustichello while both men shared a Genoese prison cell.
Skeptical Europeans dubbed his manuscript 'Il Milione', teasing him for seemingly inflating every marvel by the millions.
This Venetian merchant spent roughly seventeen years serving at the court of Kublai Khan after traversing the Silk Road.

cards.prompt: Deduce this sweeping medieval empire as the clues narrow.
cards.funFactWhy: Its diplomatic safe-conduct passports, metal tablets called paiza, let merchants travel from the Black Sea to Beijing under imperial protection.
cards.helpfulHint: Its founder took the title Genghis Khan before his grandsons pushed from Korea to Eastern Europe.

clues: Its silver-fountained capital at Karakorum hosted imperial interfaith debates among Buddhists, Muslims, and Nestorian Christians.
Its Yam relay network stationed fresh mounts every few dozen kilometers to rocket dispatches across Eurasia.
United by Temujin on the Asian steppe in 1206, it grew into the largest contiguous land empire in human history.

cards.prompt: Study this 480 BCE coastal chokepoint plate. At which narrow pass did a Greek coalition stall Xerxes I's Persian invasion for three days?
cards.funFactWhy: King Leonidas did not fight alone with 300 Spartans: roughly 7,000 Greeks held the defile at first, and 700 Thespians stayed beside them to the end.
cards.helpfulHint: Its Greek name means 'Hot Gates', honoring the warm sulfur springs steaming beside the mountain wall.

visualSpotter.caption: 480 BCE coastal defile and highland flanking trail

cards.prompt: Examine this 216 BCE double-envelopment diagram. In which Second Punic War clash did Hannibal trap and crush a far larger Roman army?
cards.funFactWhy: Hannibal intentionally bowed his thin infantry center outward so advancing Roman legions marched themselves straight into a closing U-shaped steel trap.
cards.helpfulHint: Fought beside the Aufidus River in southern Italy, it remains military academies' textbook example of tactical encirclement.

visualSpotter.caption: 216 BCE convex-to-concave double-envelopment pocket

cards.prompt: Which planet rotates on its side?
cards.funFactWhy: Tilted nearly 98 degrees, its poles spend 42 Earth years baked in nonstop sunlight followed by 42 years in pitch-black winter.
cards.helpfulHint: This pale cyan ice giant orbits just past Saturn and wears a faint vertical ring system.

cards.prompt: Which element has the symbol W?
cards.funFactWhy: Its symbol comes from the mineral wolframite, and at 3,422 degrees Celsius it boasts the highest melting point of any pure metal.
cards.helpfulHint: Its sky-high heat resistance made it the go-to filament inside classic incandescent lightbulbs.

cards.prompt: Given a mythical bathtub large enough to hold a planet, only one world in our solar system has a lower average density than liquid water and would float. Which is it?
cards.funFactWhy: Packed mostly with lightweight hydrogen and helium, its mean density of 0.69 grams per cubic centimeter makes it lighter than oak wood.
cards.helpfulHint: This gas giant is already famous for its dazzling icy ring system.

cards.prompt: In 1967, graduate student Jocelyn Bell Burnell detected radio ticks so eerily regular her lab nicknamed the source LGM-1 for Little Green Men. What had she discovered?
cards.funFactWhy: Her first signal pulsed every 1.337 seconds with atomic-clock precision, proving that collapsed stellar cores can spin like cosmic lighthouses.
cards.helpfulHint: It is a rapidly rotating, strongly magnetized neutron star whose radiation beams sweep past Earth on every spin.

cards.prompt: What counterintuitive kitchen phenomenon did Tanzanian teenager Erasto Mpemba champion in 1963 that physicists still debate in modern labs?
cards.funFactWhy: Mpemba noticed his warm ice-cream mix solidified ahead of his classmates' cooled batches, and Aristotle had actually remarked on the same quirk over two millennia earlier.
cards.helpfulHint: It defies everyday intuition about which mug of water wins a race to turn solid inside a freezer.
choices: Salt water freezes faster than fresh water
Hot water can freeze faster than cold water
Ice shrinks when cooled past minus 40 C

cards.prompt: In 1928, Paul Dirac merged quantum mechanics with special relativity in an equation that stubbornly spat out negative-energy solutions — unexpectedly predicting what?
cards.funFactWhy: Four years later, Carl Anderson spotted a cloud-chamber track curving the exact opposite way from an electron, proving the positron was real.
cards.helpfulHint: When one of these mirror-twin particles meets its ordinary counterpart, both annihilate into pure gamma-ray energy.

cards.prompt: Pair each remarkable moon of our solar system with the host planet it circles.
cards.funFactWhy: Neptune's largest moon orbits backward against its planet's spin, a smoking gun that it was once a free-roaming Kuiper Belt dwarf planet captured by gravity.
cards.helpfulHint: The hazy moon with liquid methane lakes circles the ringed giant, while the tiny potato-shaped moon skims just above the Red Planet.

match4.instruction: Match each moon to its host planet

cards.prompt: Link four foundational metric units named for famous scientists to the physical quantity each measures.
cards.funFactWhy: One unit of pressure equals just one newton spread over a full square meter — roughly the gentle weight of a single dollar bill resting flat on a table.
cards.helpfulHint: Radio stations broadcast in cycles per second, while circuit resistors are labeled with the Greek letter omega.

match4.instruction: Match each SI unit to the physical quantity it measures

cards.prompt: Match four giants of physics, chemistry, and astronomy to the landmark discovery that cemented their fame.
cards.funFactWhy: When alpha particles bounced straight back off tissue-thin gold foil, the baffled experimenter remarked it was as astonishing as firing an artillery shell at tissue paper and watching it rebound.
cards.helpfulHint: One Russian chemist boldly left empty boxes for undiscovered elements, while a Mount Wilson astronomer gave his name to NASA's most famous space telescope.

match4.instruction: Match each scientist to their landmark breakthrough

cards.prompt: Rank these four planets by average distance from the Sun, from closest to farthest.
cards.funFactWhy: Sunlight reaches the innermost of these four worlds in just six minutes, yet takes over four full hours to arrive at the outermost ice giant.
cards.helpfulHint: Think of Earth's two next-door neighbors first, followed by the ringed gas giant and the outermost major planet.

cards.prompt: Put these four milestone space launches and landings in chronological order from earliest to latest.
cards.funFactWhy: Just twelve short years separated a beach-ball-sized Soviet beeping sphere from astronauts walking across the Sea of Tranquility.
cards.helpfulHint: The first artificial satellite opened the Space Age in the 1950s, while NASA's gold-mirrored infrared observatory launched on Christmas Day in the 2020s.

cards.prompt: Order these four familiar elements by atomic number, from fewest protons to most.
cards.funFactWhy: Stars can steadily fuse lighter nuclei up through iron, but forging precious metals heavier than iron requires cataclysmic supernovae or colliding neutron stars.
cards.helpfulHint: The backbone of organic life sits in the top-right second row, while the dense yellow bullion metal sits near the bottom of the transition metals.

cards.prompt: Three of these gases belong to the aloof noble gases of Group 18. Spot the ONE imposter from a different column of the periodic table.
cards.funFactWhy: While noble gases have full valence shells and shun bonding, the odd gas out forms an ultra-strong triple bond with itself that makes up most of Earth's sky.
cards.helpfulHint: Look for the gas essential to plant fertilizers and DNA rather than glowing shop signs and welding shields.

cards.prompt: Tap ALL THREE subatomic particles that are truly elementary in the Standard Model — not built out of smaller quarks.
cards.funFactWhy: Both nuclear heavyweights and mesons are composite bundles glued together by the strong force, whereas light quanta and leptons have no known internal parts.
cards.helpfulHint: Select the particle of light plus the two leptons, and steer clear of atomic-nucleus building blocks.

cards.prompt: Three of these robotic spacecraft actually touched down on another world and transmitted from its surface. Spot the ONE imposter that only zoomed past!
cards.funFactWhy: Racing outward at roughly 50,000 kilometers per hour, the Pluto explorer carried nowhere near enough fuel to brake into orbit and snapped its heart-shaped basin photos on the fly.
cards.helpfulHint: One of these missions screamed past a distant Kuiper Belt dwarf planet in 2015 without ever touching down.

cards.prompt: Earth's dry air is mostly nitrogen, not oxygen. Dial in the approximate percentage of dry air made up of nitrogen.
cards.funFactWhy: Oxygen clocks in at just under 21 percent, while argon sneaks into third place at nearly 1 percent — over twenty times more abundant than carbon dioxide.
cards.helpfulHint: Subtract roughly one-fifth for oxygen and a tiny sliver for argon and trace gases from 100 percent.

cards.prompt: How many officially confirmed chemical elements currently fill out the seven complete rows of the IUPAC periodic table?
cards.funFactWhy: Element 118, oganesson, completes the noble-gas column, though physicists have synthesized only a handful of its atoms and each decays in under a millisecond.
cards.helpfulHint: It sits just shy of 120, finishing the seventh period cleanly with four elements named in 2016.

cards.prompt: Absolute zero — 0 Kelvin — marks the theoretical thermal floor of the universe. Dial in its value in degrees Celsius (to the nearest whole degree).
cards.funFactWhy: Although quantum zero-point jitters keep atoms from freezing completely motionless, ultracold laser traps on Earth have chilled gas clouds to billionths of a degree above this floor.
cards.helpfulHint: Water freezes at 273.15 Kelvin, so simply flip that offset below zero on the Celsius scale.

cards.prompt: Identify this blistering neighboring world as the clues intensify.
cards.funFactWhy: Because it rotates lazily backward relative to most planets, the Sun actually rises in the west and sets in the east above its suffocating clouds.
cards.helpfulHint: It orbits inside Earth's track and shines brighter in our twilight sky than any star.

clues: One full spin around its axis takes longer than its entire orbital trip around the Sun.
Its crushing carbon-dioxide atmosphere mimics the pressure 900 meters beneath Earth's ocean under clouds laced with sulfuric acid.
Named for the Roman goddess of love, it is the hottest planet in our solar system even though Mercury sits closer to the Sun.

cards.prompt: Name this charismatic Nobel laureate before Clue 3 seals it.
cards.funFactWhy: He drove a beige van painted head-to-toe with his own looping particle sketches and customized its California license plate to read 'QANTUM'.
cards.helpfulHint: His memoir famously asks, 'Surely You're Joking, Mr. ...?'

clues: While picking classified combination safes as a prank at Los Alamos, he also played bongo drums and translated Mayan glyphs for fun.
During televised 1986 Challenger hearings, he clamped a rubber O-ring into a cup of ice water to show how freezing launch temperatures doomed the shuttle.
He shared the 1965 Nobel Prize in Physics for quantum electrodynamics and lent his name to the iconic line-and-squiggle particle interaction diagrams.

cards.prompt: Identify this faint universal signal as the clues escalate.
cards.funFactWhy: Roughly one percent of the fuzzy static snow on an old untuned analog television came directly from this primordial afterglow.
cards.helpfulHint: Every direction in deep space bathes us in this 2.7-Kelvin leftover light from the infant universe.

clues: In 1964, Bell Labs astronomers Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson initially blamed this stubborn, uniform hiss on pigeon droppings coating their horn antenna.
Its near-perfect blackbody spectrum glows at an ultra-frigid 2.725 Kelvin uniformly across every patch of the sky.
Released roughly 380,000 years after the Big Bang when newborn atoms turned space transparent, it is the oldest electromagnetic afterglow we can detect.

cards.prompt: Inspect this methylxanthine alkaloid blueprint (C8H10N4O2). Which everyday stimulant powers billions of mornings by blocking adenosine fatigue receptors?
cards.funFactWhy: Plants evolved this bitter alkaloid as a natural pesticide to paralyze leaf-chewing insects — humans simply brewed nature's bug spray into espresso.
cards.helpfulHint: You will find this nitrogen-rich molecule naturally tucked inside coffee beans, tea leaves, and cacao pods.

visualSpotter.caption: Methylxanthine alkaloid skeleton with formula C8H10N4O2

cards.prompt: Study this star chart of the smallest of all 88 official constellations. Which kite-shaped pattern shines on the national flags of Australia, New Zealand, and Brazil?
cards.funFactWhy: Though it covers a modest 68 square degrees of sky, four of its stars gleam brighter than magnitude 2.8, making it the brightest constellation per square degree.
cards.helpfulHint: Southern Hemisphere sailors extend its longer axis four-and-a-half times southward to pinpoint the South Celestial Pole.

visualSpotter.caption: Smallest of 88 constellations at declination -60 degrees

cards.prompt: What is the capital of Australia?
cards.funFactWhy: Rather than letting fierce rivals Sydney and Melbourne win the honor, lawmakers commissioned a brand-new planned city inland between them in 1913.
cards.helpfulHint: It is neither the city of the iconic shell-roofed Opera House nor the home of the Australian Open.

cards.prompt: Which desert spans northern Chile's coast?
cards.funFactWhy: Blocked from moisture by both the towering Andes and a frigid Pacific current, some of its weather stations have gone decades without a single measurable raindrop.
cards.helpfulHint: NASA tests prototype Mars rovers on this arid South American plateau because its soil mimics the Red Planet.

cards.prompt: Which African nation completely encircles the mountain kingdom of Lesotho, making Lesotho an enclave surrounded by just one neighbor?
cards.funFactWhy: Only three sovereign states on Earth are completely enclosed by a single country — Vatican City and San Marino inside Italy, plus Lesotho inside this southern giant.
cards.helpfulHint: Its territory wraps around the Drakensberg highlands and boasts three separate capitals: Pretoria, Cape Town, and Bloemfontein.

cards.prompt: Despite stretching roughly 5,000 kilometers across five geographical time zones from east to west, which nation keeps its entire mainland on a single official clock?
cards.funFactWhy: Because the whole country runs on UTC+8, residents in far-western Kashgar routinely watch summer daylight linger past 10:30 PM on the official wall clock.
cards.helpfulHint: Every wristwatch from Shanghai to Tibet officially synchronizes with the clock in Beijing.

cards.prompt: Only two countries on Earth are doubly landlocked, requiring travelers to cross at least two international borders to reach an open ocean. Liechtenstein is one; what is the other?
cards.funFactWhy: Every single one of its five neighbors — Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Afghanistan, and Turkmenistan — is itself cut off from the world's open oceans.
cards.helpfulHint: Home to the turquoise-tiled Silk Road cities of Samarkand and Bukhara, it sits right in the heart of Central Asia.

cards.prompt: Measured from the center of the Earth rather than sea level, which Andean volcano's summit reaches more than two kilometers farther into space than Mount Everest?
cards.funFactWhy: Because Earth's spin makes the planet bulge roughly 21 kilometers wider at the Equator than at the poles, this equatorial peak steals Everest's crown for farthest point from Earth's core.
cards.helpfulHint: Rising just south of the Equator in Ecuador, its snow-capped cone dominates the nation's coat of arms.

cards.prompt: Connect four legendary rivers to the ocean or sea into which each finally empties.
cards.funFactWhy: The Amazon pumps so much freshwater past its mouth that sailors 150 kilometers out at sea can still dip a bucket and taste diluted, slightly fresh water.
cards.helpfulHint: Egypt's river delta fans northward toward Europe, while central Europe's river flows east past Vienna and Budapest.

match4.instruction: Match each river to the sea or ocean where it empties

cards.prompt: Match four national capitals — none of which is its country's most populous city — to the nation it governs.
cards.funFactWhy: Architect Oscar Niemeyer and planner Lucio Costa shaped Brazil's purpose-built inland capital in 1960 so that from the air its avenues resemble an airplane or soaring bird.
cards.helpfulHint: One sits on the windy Cook Strait in the South Pacific, while another was chosen by Queen Victoria along the Rideau Canal.

match4.instruction: Match each capital city to its country

cards.prompt: Pair four jaw-dropping natural landmarks with the country (or border nations) you must visit to see them.
cards.funFactWhy: After a thin rain, Bolivia's high-altitude salt crust becomes a 10,000-square-kilometer natural mirror so optically flat that orbital satellites use it to calibrate their altimeters.
cards.helpfulHint: Mosi-oa-Tunya means 'The Smoke That Thunders' in southern Africa, and Pamukkale translates to 'Cotton Castle' in Anatolian Turkish.

match4.instruction: Match each natural wonder to its home country

cards.prompt: Rank these four great oceans by surface area, from smallest to largest.
cards.funFactWhy: Earth's largest ocean basin is so colossal that every landmass on the planet could fit inside it with room to spare for an extra Africa.
cards.helpfulHint: The polar sea around the North Pole is the compact one, and the mighty basin bordering Japan and California dwarfs the rest.

cards.prompt: Order these four famous mountain summits by elevation above sea level, from shortest to tallest.
cards.funFactWhy: North America's Alaskan giant edges out Africa's tallest volcano by nearly 300 meters, though the Tanzanian peak holds the crown as Earth's tallest free-standing mountain.
cards.helpfulHint: Japan's sacred volcano sits well under 4,000 meters, and the Alaskan peak just tops Tanzania's snow-crowned summit.

cards.prompt: Arrange these four sovereign nations by total area, from smallest to largest.
cards.funFactWhy: The two European microstates combined are still smaller than New York's Central Park, yet they command two distinct United Nations footprints.
cards.helpfulHint: The walled papal enclave inside Rome is the tiniest nation on Earth, followed by the Riviera Grand Prix principality and Southeast Asia's island city-state.

cards.prompt: Tap ALL THREE nations whose territory is sliced directly by the Equator (0 degrees latitude).
cards.funFactWhy: Out of 195 countries on Earth, only 13 touch the Equator, and one of them even named itself after the imaginary line.
cards.helpfulHint: Pick one nation in the northern Andes, one safari stronghold in East Africa, and Southeast Asia's sprawling archipelago.

cards.prompt: Three of these North African capitals look out over the Mediterranean Sea. Spot the ONE imposter that faces the Atlantic Ocean instead.
cards.funFactWhy: While Morocco has both Mediterranean and Atlantic coastlines, its royal capital sits on the open Atlantic right beside the mouth of the Bou Regreg river.
cards.helpfulHint: Picture the Maghreb from east to west: the westernmost kingdom puts its capital on the Atlantic side past Gibraltar.

cards.prompt: Tap ALL THREE nations whose continuous mainland physically straddles both Europe and Asia.
cards.funFactWhy: West of the Ural River, a sweeping corner of Central Asia's largest nation sits geographically in Europe — big enough on its own to outsize Greece.
cards.helpfulHint: Look for the giant spanning eleven time zones, the republic crossing the Bosporus, and the Central Asian steppe nation sliced by the Ural River.

cards.prompt: Africa contains more sovereign nations than any other continent. Dial in the exact count of UN-recognized countries in Africa.
cards.funFactWhy: South Sudan became the continent's newest member in 2011, pushing the total past Europe's forty-plus countries by a comfortable margin.
cards.helpfulHint: It is slightly more than the number of U.S. states, and right in the mid-fifties.

cards.prompt: Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench plunges farther below sea level than Mount Everest rises above it. Dial in its approximate depth in meters (to the nearest 100 m).
cards.funFactWhy: If you dropped Mount Everest straight into this Pacific chasm, its snowy summit would still be buried more than two kilometers underwater.
cards.helpfulHint: Add roughly 2,000 meters to Mount Everest's 8,849-meter height.

cards.prompt: Stretching from Baltic Kaliningrad to Pacific Kamchatka, how many official time zones does Russia currently span?
cards.funFactWhy: Russia briefly trimmed itself down to nine zones in 2010 before reversing course in 2014 to restore its sweeping eleven-zone span.
cards.helpfulHint: It is almost half of the 24 hourly slices around the globe, spanning from UTC+2 all the way to UTC+12.

cards.prompt: Identify this dramatic North Atlantic nation before Clue 3 seals the deal.
cards.funFactWhy: Because its subarctic ocean climate freezes and thaws unpredictably, mosquito pupae can never finish a full life cycle — keeping the island blissfully bite-free.
cards.helpfulHint: Its sagas were written by Norse settlers who named it with a chilly twist compared to its far icier neighbor.

clues: It is famously free of wild mosquitoes, and its national parliament, the Althing, first gathered outdoors on a rift-valley plain in 930 CE.
Volcanic geothermal energy warms almost all of its homes, powered by the Mid-Atlantic Ridge tearing the island slowly in two.
Home to Reykjavik, the world's northernmost capital of a sovereign nation, it is known as the Land of Fire and Ice.

cards.prompt: Identify this extraordinary freshwater giant as the clues climb.
cards.funFactWhy: Its crystal-clear winter ice freezes thick enough to carry heavy trucks and even temporary railway tracks during the 1904 Russo-Japanese War.
cards.helpfulHint: It is Earth's deepest and oldest freshwater lake, curving like a giant blue crescent across southern Russia.

clues: It shelters the nerpa, the only exclusively freshwater species of seal living anywhere on Earth.
More than 300 rivers pour into its rift-valley trough, yet only one river — the Angara — flows back out.
Plunging 1,642 meters deep in southern Siberia, it holds roughly one-fifth of all unfrozen surface freshwater on the planet.

cards.prompt: Deduce this otherworldly island group from three escalating clues.
cards.funFactWhy: Ancient Mediterranean traders prized its crimson dragon's blood tree resin as a miraculous medicine, incense, and luxury red dye for violins.
cards.helpfulHint: Guarding the Horn of Africa in the Arabian Sea, its surreal umbrella-shaped trees look straight off a sci-fi movie set.

clues: Over a third of its plant species grow nowhere else on Earth, led by umbrella-shaped dragon's blood trees that weep crimson sap.
Administered by Yemen, it sits closer to Somalia than to the Arabian Peninsula right at the mouth of the Gulf of Aden.
Dubbed the 'Galapagos of the Indian Ocean', this UNESCO World Heritage archipelago shares its name with its largest island.

cards.prompt: Inspect this 1914 elevation diagram showing three-step hydraulic locks lifting vessels 26 meters over an isthmus. Which famed canal links the Atlantic and Pacific?
cards.funFactWhy: Thanks to the isthmus's quirky S-curve, ships traveling from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific actually head southeast through the locks.
cards.helpfulHint: Its elevated freshwater Gatun Lake powers gravity-fed chambers across Central America's narrowest waist.

visualSpotter.caption: 82 km isthmus lock elevation profile (+26 m summit lake)

cards.prompt: Spot the pin placed directly on the Bosporus Strait connecting the Black Sea and Sea of Marmara. Which historic transcontinental metropolis sits beneath the marker?
cards.funFactWhy: Over sixteen centuries it served consecutively as the imperial seat of the Roman, Byzantine, Latin, and Ottoman empires.
cards.helpfulHint: Daily commuters here routinely take a fifteen-minute boat ride from Europe to Asia just to get to work.

visualSpotter.caption: 41.0 N, 29.0 E on the maritime bridge between Europe and Asia

cards.prompt: Who painted The Starry Night?
cards.funFactWhy: He painted the swirling 1889 nocturnal sky from memory inside his asylum room, inventing a nostalgic Dutch-style church steeple that was never outside his barred window.
cards.helpfulHint: This Dutch Post-Impressionist also immortalized bright yellow sunflowers and his own bandaged ear.

cards.prompt: Which museum houses the Mona Lisa?

cards.helpfulHint: One of these four icons packs falling four-square geometric pieces rather than Italian plumbers, yellow dot-eaters, or Hyrule dungeons.

cards.prompt: If a ten-pin bowler chains together twelve consecutive strikes across all ten frames, what flawless perfect score lights up the scoreboard?
cards.funFactWhy: Because each strike adds the next two rolls to its frame, every frame maxes out at 30 points — and the tenth frame grants two bonus throws to finish the math.
cards.helpfulHint: Multiply ten frames by the 30-point maximum per frame.

cards.prompt: On March 2, 1962, Philadelphia Warriors center Wilt Chamberlain erupted for the single greatest scoring game in NBA history against the Knicks. Dial in his exact point total.
cards.funFactWhy: No television cameras recorded the night in Hershey, Pennsylvania — only radio audio and the iconic locker-room photo of Wilt holding a piece of paper scribbled with his round-number feat.
cards.helpfulHint: It is basketball's mythical triple-digit milestone, which Kobe Bryant later chased all the way to 81.

cards.prompt: Every official Major League Baseball is hand-stitched with waxed red thread around two figure-eight cowhide panels. Dial in the exact number of double stitches on a regulation ball.
cards.funFactWhy: By eerie baseball poetry, that exact stitch count matched the 108-year championship drought the Chicago Cubs finally snapped in Game 7 of the 2016 World Series.
cards.helpfulHint: It sits just above 100 — and famously matched the exact number of years between Chicago Cubs World Series titles.

cards.prompt: Identify this towering sprint legend as the clues pick up speed.
cards.funFactWhy: At 1.95 meters tall, he needed only 41 long strides to cover 100 meters while shorter rivals took 44 or 45 steps to finish behind him.
cards.helpfulHint: His signature victory celebration points skyward like an archer aiming an arrow into the stadium lights.

clues: Before choosing track and field, he dreamed of becoming a fast bowler on the cricket pitch in Sherwood Content, Jamaica.
In the 2008 Beijing Olympic final, he slowed down and thumped his chest well before the finish line yet still broke the 100-meter world record.
Nicknamed 'Lightning', this eight-time Olympic gold medalist blasted through 100 meters in an astonishing 9.58 seconds in Berlin in 2009.

cards.prompt: Name this legendary family board game before Clue 3 gives it away.
cards.funFactWhy: Over 300 million sets have been printed in dozens of languages, yet house rules like putting tax fines under Free Parking actually double the average playtime.
cards.helpfulHint: Its mascot sports a top hat, tuxedo, and bright white mustache while players argue over blue real estate.

clues: Its 1904 precursor, 'The Landlord's Game', was patented by activist Elizabeth Magie as an economic warning against greedy rent hoarding.
During World War II, British intelligence hid real silk escape maps, miniature compasses, and genuine currency inside special editions mailed to Allied POWs.
Named after Atlantic City streets, its metallic thimble, top hat, and battleship tokens circle past 'Go', railroads, and pricey Boardwalk hotels.

cards.prompt: Identify this jaw-dropping multi-sport pioneer as the clues escalate.
cards.funFactWhy: Besides Olympic track glory and ten major golf titles, she was an All-American basketball player, pitched in a Major League exhibition game, and once claimed she could beat almost anyone at billiards too.
cards.helpfulHint: She shared her legendary first-name nickname with baseball's Sultan of Swat after blasting five home runs in a childhood game.

clues: At the 1932 AAU track championships, she entered eight of ten events as a one-woman squad for a Dallas insurance company and took first place in six to outscore entire 20-athlete teams solo.
Weeks later at the 1932 Los Angeles Olympics, she won gold in the 80-meter hurdles and javelin, losing high-jump gold only when judges ruled her Western roll an illegal dive.
Named the Associated Press's top female athlete of the first half of the 20th century, she later co-founded the LPGA and captured ten major golf titles.

cards.prompt: Study this 1912 diamond blueprint featuring a short 310-foot left-field line guarded by a sheer 37-foot wall. Which storied MLB ballpark is plotted here?
cards.funFactWhy: Built to stop Lansdowne Street neighbors from sneaking free glimpses and to turn cheap pop flies into noisy singles, the 37-foot wall stayed plastered in tin ads until it was painted green in 1947.
cards.helpfulHint: Home of the Boston Red Sox since 1912, it is the oldest active stadium in Major League Baseball.

cards.prompt: Inspect this 1995 ballpark survey featuring cavernous outfield dimensions and a Row 20 marker sitting exactly 5,280 feet above sea level. Which high-altitude MLB stadium is shown?
cards.funFactWhy: Because thin Rocky Mountain air lets baseballs carry roughly nine percent farther, MLB stores every game ball here inside a climate-controlled humidor so they do not dry out like golf balls.
cards.helpfulHint: Set in downtown Denver, Row 20 of its upper deck is painted purple to trace exactly one mile above sea level.

visualSpotter.caption: Opened 1995; 5,200 ft field elevation with a 5,280 ft Row 20 stripe

cards.prompt: Which HTTP code means page missing?
cards.funFactWhy: HTTP 404 has spawned its own internet art genre, though contrary to urban legend it was never named after a mysterious CERN office room.
cards.helpfulHint: It sits in the 400 client-error family and reads the same forward and backward.

cards.prompt: What insect inspired the computer bug?
cards.funFactWhy: Harvard Mark II engineers taped a real moth pulled from Relay 70 into their 1947 logbook, quipping it was the first actual case of a bug being found.
cards.helpfulHint: This nocturnal cousin of the butterfly is famously drawn toward warm glowing lights.

cards.prompt: Which British comedy inspired Python's name?
cards.funFactWhy: Guido van Rossum was reading scripts from the anarchic BBC sketch troupe in December 1989 and wanted a name that felt short, punchy, and slightly irreverent.
cards.helpfulHint: Its absurd sketches gave us the Ministry of Silly Walks and the Dead Parrot.

cards.prompt: Bluetooth borrows its name from Harald Gormsson, a 10th-century king who united which two Scandinavian realms?
cards.funFactWhy: Just as Harald bridged rival Viking tribes, engineers wanted one wireless standard to unite phones and PCs, even fusing his Nordic initials into the logo.
cards.helpfulHint: One realm sits on the Jutland Peninsula while its fjord-carved neighbor stretches north across the Skagerrak.

cards.prompt: Despite 'Graphics' opening the acronym, GIF creator Steve Wilhite insisted it rhymes with what pantry staple?
cards.funFactWhy: CompuServe's early developers even riffed on a famous TV ad slogan by joking that 'choosy developers choose GIF.'
cards.helpfulHint: Think of a creamy American sandwich spread whose soft initial consonant sparked an endless online pronunciation war.

cards.prompt: Alan Turing's landmark 1936 paper proved no universal algorithm can inspect an arbitrary program and always tell what?
cards.funFactWhy: Turing's proof by contradiction works like a mischievous liar paradox that forces any supposed oracle program to do the exact opposite of its own prediction.
cards.helpfulHint: The question isn't about speed or memory — it's whether the code ever finishes running at all.
choices: How much memory it will allocate
Which compiler built its machine code
Whether its network traffic is encrypted

cards.helpfulHint: A crustacean's iron-rich nickname links to a memory-safe systems language, while a tentacled feline guards millions of code repositories.

cards.prompt: Order these iconic Apple hardware debuts chronologically from earliest launch to most recent.
cards.funFactWhy: Apple's 1984 Super Bowl commercial for the Macintosh aired nationally just once during the game, yet became one of advertising's most studied spots.
cards.helpfulHint: The desktop box came in the Orwellian eighties, while the pocket music player arrived six years ahead of the touchscreen phone.

cards.prompt: Stack these nostalgic physical storage formats from smallest standard capacity to largest.
cards.funFactWhy: A single 25-gigabyte Blu-ray disc holds more data than 17,000 classic 3.5-inch floppy disks stacked into a tower taller than a ten-story building.
cards.helpfulHint: Follow the media evolution from the magnetic 'Save' icon through shiny music discs to blue-violet laser video.

cards.prompt: Line up these four watershed moments in computing history from earliest breakthrough to latest.
cards.funFactWhy: The first ARPANET message tried to send 'LOGIN' from UCLA to Stanford in 1969, but the system crashed after just two letters, making 'LO' the internet's accidental greeting.
cards.helpfulHint: Solid-state electronics started right after World War II, while decentralized cryptocurrency emerged in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis.

cards.prompt: Pick the THREE genuine programming languages hiding among three completely made-up imposters.
cards.funFactWhy: Kotlin was named after Kotlin Island near St. Petersburg, echoing how Java had taken its name from an Indonesian island famous for coffee.
cards.helpfulHint: Look for a red gemstone used on Rails, Google's preferred Android language, and a functional language named after a logician.

cards.prompt: Three of these alphabet-soup protocols actually run today's internet — spot the ONE bogus acronym.
cards.funFactWhy: BGP is essentially the postal routing directory of the entire internet, which is why a single typo in a BGP table can briefly take global platforms offline.
cards.helpfulHint: Real internet standards handle everyday mail, IP leases, and routing — none rely on sci-fi subatomic buzzwords.

cards.prompt: Select the THREE computing titans who actually received the A.M. Turing Award — often called the Nobel Prize of computing.
cards.funFactWhy: Grace Hopper and Linus Torvalds are towering legends who never received the Turing Award, though the ACM named its prestigious young-innovator prize in Hopper's honor.
cards.helpfulHint: Count out anyone who lived in the 19th century, and remember that Unix's co-creator, the author of 'The Art of Computer Programming', and the pioneer of data abstraction all won.

cards.prompt: Dial in the year Steve Jobs walked onstage at Macworld to unveil the very first iPhone.
cards.funFactWhy: During that famous keynote, Jobs secretly swapped among several prototype handsets backstage because no single unit could finish every demo without crashing.
cards.helpfulHint: It debuted in January, six years after the original iPod and one year before the App Store opened.

cards.prompt: How many distinct numerical values can a single standard 8-bit unsigned byte represent?
cards.funFactWhy: Because computer counts begin at zero, an 8-bit color channel maxes out at 255 even though it encodes one more total shade than that.
cards.helpfulHint: Double the number 2 eight times in a row — it's also the exact number of shades per RGB channel in classic web color.

cards.prompt: Dial in the year Tim Berners-Lee submitted his CERN proposal that launched the World Wide Web.
cards.funFactWhy: His supervisor Mike Sendall scribbled 'Vague, but exciting...' across the cover of that March proposal — arguably history's greatest understatement.
cards.helpfulHint: It happened in the same eventful year the Berlin Wall came down.

cards.prompt: Identify this ubiquitous human-interface design from three escalating clues.
cards.funFactWhy: Despite modern touchscreens having zero metal levers to jam, this 19th-century compromise remains so deeply ingrained in human muscle memory that faster rivals rarely stick.
cards.helpfulHint: Glance down at the upper-left corner of an English laptop keyboard.

clues: Patented in 1878 by Christopher Latham Sholes, this arrangement separated common English letter pairs to keep brass typebars from tangling.
Every single letter needed to spell the word 'TYPEWRITER' sits conveniently on its top alphabetic row.
It takes its name straight from the first six letters along the top-left row of standard English keyboards.

cards.prompt: Name this visionary 19th-century computing pioneer before the final clue drops.
cards.funFactWhy: The U.S. Department of Defense honored her in 1980 by naming a high-reliability programming language used in avionics and satellites after her first name.
cards.helpfulHint: Her estranged father was the flamboyant British Romantic poet Lord Byron.

clues: Her 1843 'Note G' charted a looping algorithm to calculate Bernoulli numbers for a brass engine that was never finished.
She imagined general-purpose machines weaving music and abstract symbols just as a Jacquard loom weaves floral patterns.
Collaborator of Charles Babbage on the Analytical Engine, widely celebrated as history's first computer programmer.

cards.prompt: Identify this legendary vacuum-tube computer from three escalating clues.
cards.funFactWhy: Because vacuum tubes blew out almost daily, engineers kept a shopping cart of spare tubes on standby — and discovered that simply leaving the power on dramatically reduced burnout.
cards.helpfulHint: Its five-letter acronym opens with 'Electronic Numerical Integrator' and lives in Philadelphia computing lore.

clues: Weighing roughly 30 tons and drawing 150 kilowatts across 17,468 vacuum tubes, it had to be programmed by physically plugging cables across giant patch panels.
Built at the University of Pennsylvania to speed up artillery tables, its six original programmers were all women whose work went unsung for decades.
Unveiled in February 1946 as the first programmable, electronic, general-purpose digital computer.

cards.prompt: Study this 1945 stored-program blueprint — routing instructions and data over one shared bus defines what famous computer architecture?
cards.funFactWhy: Modern CPUs hide this classic shared-bus bottleneck with multi-level L1, L2, and L3 caches that keep frequently used instructions and data close to the core.
cards.helpfulHint: It bears the surname of the Hungarian-American polymath who drafted the 1945 EDVAC report.

visualSpotter.caption: Stored-program architecture with unified memory and shared data bus

cards.prompt: Check the truth table on this two-gate schematic: an XOR gate produces Sum (S) while an AND gate produces Carry (C). What binary circuit is this?
cards.funFactWhy: Chain two of these little circuits together with an OR gate and you get a full adder — the microscopic building block of every calculator and CPU.
cards.helpfulHint: It sums two single bits cleanly, but gets its fractional name because it has no input pin for an incoming carry.

visualSpotter.caption: Two-input binary combinational gate diagram with truth table

cards.prompt: How many hearts does an octopus have?
cards.funFactWhy: Two pump blood across its gills while the third supplies the rest of its body — and actually pauses beating while the octopus swims, which is why they prefer crawling.
cards.helpfulHint: Count one for each pair of gill sides plus one central pump for the rest of its body.

cards.prompt: Which bird can genuinely fly backward?
cards.funFactWhy: Its shoulder joint swivels almost 180 degrees so its wings trace a horizontal figure-eight, generating lift on both the forward and backward strokes.
cards.helpfulHint: This nectar-sipping miniature acrobat beats its wings up to 80 times a second.

cards.prompt: Which venomous Australian mammal lays eggs?
cards.funFactWhy: When the first preserved specimen reached London in 1799, British naturalists tried prying off its duck-like bill with scissors, convinced a prankster had sewn animals together.
cards.helpfulHint: Males carry venomous spurs on their hind ankles and hunt underwater with electroreceptors in their rubbery bills.

cards.prompt: A gathering of crows is famously a 'murder,' while a show-stopping flock of bright pink flamingos goes by what dazzling collective noun?
cards.funFactWhy: Flamingos are actually born dull gray and earn their neon blush only from beta-carotene pigments packed inside the algae and brine shrimp they filter-feed.
cards.helpfulHint: The word shares its root with an adjective meaning extravagantly bold, showy, and impossible to ignore.

cards.prompt: Why do Australian wombats — uniquely among all known animals — produce neat cube-shaped droppings?
cards.funFactWhy: Biophysicists won the 2019 Ig Nobel Prize in Physics for proving that alternating stiff and stretchy bands inside the wombat's intestine sculpt those crisp 90-degree edges.
cards.helpfulHint: Imagine leaving a scent signpost perched atop a slanted log or boulder in the bush.
choices: They perch them on rocks and logs as markers that will not roll away
Their flat molars chew eucalyptus bark into tiny square tiles
They mortar their burrow entrances with sun-baked cubes
The sharp corners stop hungry dingoes from sniffing their trail

cards.prompt: Which heat-loving bacterium plucked from a scalding Wyoming hot spring gave science the enzyme that revolutionized PCR DNA amplification?
cards.funFactWhy: Because its Taq polymerase shrugs off near-boiling temperatures, labs no longer had to hand-pipette fresh enzyme after every single heating cycle of DNA copying.
cards.helpfulHint: Its two-word Latin name translates literally to 'heat' and 'of water,' and gives its initials to Taq polymerase.

cards.prompt: Pair each record-breaking creature with the biological superlative that puts it in the natural-history hall of fame.
cards.funFactWhy: A blue whale's tongue alone weighs as much as an adult Asian elephant, yet its throat is barely wide enough to swallow a grapefruit.
cards.helpfulHint: One microscopic 'water bear' curls into a glass-like tun state to laugh off cosmic radiation, while one raptor plunges past 320 km/h.

cards.helpfulHint: Think blood sugar regulation, fat emulsification, circadian sleep cues, and the fight-or-flight rush.

cards.prompt: Arrange these four mammals in order from shortest typical pregnancy (gestation) to longest.
cards.funFactWhy: An African elephant calf develops for nearly 22 months inside the womb so it can emerge weighing around 100 kilograms and stand up within an hour of birth.
cards.helpfulHint: In mammals, gestation length scales roughly with adult body size — from less than three weeks to nearly two full years.

cards.prompt: Place these landmark chapters in the history of life on Earth from earliest appearance to most recent.
cards.funFactWhy: If Earth's entire 4.5-billion-year story were compressed into a single 24-hour day, modern humans wouldn't show up until roughly six seconds before midnight.
cards.helpfulHint: Microbes ruled alone for billions of years before shelled marine animals diversified, dinosaurs walked the Triassic, and our own species arrived.

cards.prompt: Order these four mammals from slowest average resting heart rate to fastest (beats per minute).
cards.funFactWhy: Biologists joke about the 'billion-heartbeat rule': most mammals from tiny rodents to giant elephants average roughly one billion heartbeats across a natural lifespan, with humans outliving the curve thanks to medicine.
cards.helpfulHint: Smaller mammals burn heat much faster per gram of body mass, forcing their hearts to race dramatically quicker.

cards.prompt: Botanists love ruining grocery-store logic: three of these are true botanical berries, while ONE is an imposter.
cards.funFactWhy: Because a true berry grows from a single ovary with seeds embedded inside its flesh, bananas and watermelons pass the test while strawberries — whose tiny 'seeds' are actually individual fruits on a swollen stem base — fail.
cards.helpfulHint: Ironically, the imposter is the only one that actually puts the word 'berry' right in its English name.

cards.prompt: If it bites you and you die, it's venomous; if you bite it and die, it's poisonous. Select the THREE genuinely VENOMOUS creatures.
cards.funFactWhy: The adorable big-eyed slow loris is the world's only known venomous primate — it licks a toxin-secreting gland on its inner elbow to coat its teeth before biting rivals.
cards.helpfulHint: Skip the bright warning-colored frog, the sushi-hazard fish, and the milkweed butterfly — all three defend passively rather than injecting toxins.

cards.prompt: Three of these creatures pump blue, copper-based hemocyanin instead of iron-rich red blood — spot the ONE red-blooded imposter.
cards.funFactWhy: Horseshoe crab blue blood contains clotting cells so sensitive to bacterial endotoxins that pharmaceutical labs have used it since the 1970s to safety-test vaccines and IV fluids.
cards.helpfulHint: All three blue-blooded creatures are invertebrates (arthropods and mollusks), leaving one warm-blooded vertebrate out of place.

cards.prompt: Dial in the number of bones in a typical adult human skeleton after childhood bones fuse together.
cards.funFactWhy: Human babies actually enter the world with around 270 to 300 soft bones and cartilage pieces, more than a quarter of which live in your hands and feet once fused.
cards.helpfulHint: It sits just above two hundred — and remember, a full quarter of the total hides inside your two feet alone.

cards.prompt: Dial in the year Charles Darwin finally published 'On the Origin of Species' after sitting on his notes for two decades.
cards.funFactWhy: Darwin rushed the book to print only after receiving an unsettling 1858 letter from Alfred Russel Wallace independently outlining nearly the exact same theory of natural selection.
cards.helpfulHint: It hit London bookshops just two years before the American Civil War began.

cards.prompt: A giraffe's neck can stretch over six feet tall — dial in how many neck vertebrae (cervical bones) it actually contains.
cards.funFactWhy: Almost every mammal from a tiny mouse to a human to a towering giraffe shares the exact same cervical bone count — the giraffe simply stretched each bone to nearly a foot long.
cards.helpfulHint: Resist the urge to dial high: evolution recycled the exact same number sitting in your own neck right now.

cards.prompt: Identify this medical-marvel creature from three escalating clues.
cards.funFactWhy: Its genome is roughly ten times longer than a human's, packed with genetic blueprints that let scar-free limb regeneration work like biological magic.
cards.helpfulHint: Its Aztec-derived name ends in '-tl' and belongs to a critically endangered resident of Lake Xochimilco.

clues: Critically endangered in the wild canals around Mexico City, it can cleanly regrow lost legs, severed spinal cords, and even portions of its own heart and brain.
Through a developmental twist called neoteny, it reaches adulthood without ever losing its feathery external gills or leaving the water.
Affectionately misnamed the 'Mexican walking fish,' this perpetually smiling pale pink amphibian is actually a salamander.

cards.prompt: Name this microscopic cellular celebrity before the internet's favorite catchphrase gives it away.
cards.funFactWhy: Because sperm cells discard almost all of theirs at fertilization, tracing mutations in this organelle's circular DNA lets geneticists map unbroken maternal lineages back tens of thousands of years.
cards.helpfulHint: Think of the double-membraned organelle that runs cellular respiration inside almost every eukaryotic cell.

clues: Bearing their own tiny circular DNA passed almost exclusively down the maternal line, they began over a billion years ago as independent bacteria engulfed by an ancestral host cell.
Their intricately folded inner membranes, called cristae, spin molecular proton turbines that synthesize ATP nonstop.
Every high-school biology meme recites their famous six-word resume: 'the powerhouse of the cell.'

cards.prompt: Identify Earth's heaviest known living organism from three escalating clues.
cards.funFactWhy: Every autumn, all 47,000 genetically identical stems across its Utah hillside turn golden yellow nearly in unison because they are literally branches of one giant underground individual.
cards.helpfulHint: Its short Latin name translates directly to 'I spread,' and it stands in Utah's Fishlake National Forest.

clues: Blanketing roughly 106 acres of Utah's Fishlake National Forest and weighing around 6,000 metric tons, all 47,000 of its trunks share one continuous underground root network.
Its five-letter Latin name means 'I spread,' fitting a single male clonal organism that may have sprouted back near the end of the last Ice Age.
Nicknamed 'The Trembling Giant,' this sprawling quaking aspen colony is widely recognized as Earth's heaviest single living organism.

cards.funFactWhy: An active human body recycles roughly its own entire body weight in this molecule every single day, recharging each molecule hundreds of times over.
cards.helpfulHint: Count the three phosphorus atoms labeled alpha, beta, and gamma chained onto a five-carbon sugar ring.

cards.funFactWhy: Once wolves returned after a 70-year absence, elk stopped overgrazing valley stream banks, allowing aspen and willow groves to rebound and stabilize eroding riverbanks.
cards.helpfulHint: Established in 1872 atop a supervolcano caldera mostly in Wyoming, it became the world's first national park.

visualSpotter.caption: Northern Rocky Mountain geothermal basin and ecological reserve

cards.prompt: Where is the United Nations headquartered?
cards.funFactWhy: The 18-acre riverfront complex sits on land bought with an $8.5 million gift from John D. Rockefeller Jr. and operates as international territory with its own postal stamps.
cards.helpfulHint: Look along Manhattan's East River, not the Swiss lakeside city that hosts many UN agencies.

cards.prompt: Which European city hosts NATO's headquarters?
cards.funFactWhy: NATO originally operated out of London and then Paris before packing up for Belgium in 1967 after Charles de Gaulle pulled France out of the alliance's integrated command.
cards.helpfulHint: It is also the de facto administrative capital of the European Union — and famous for waffles.

cards.prompt: What Latin writ challenges unlawful detention?
cards.funFactWhy: Translating literally to 'you shall have the body,' the centuries-old safeguard forces jailers to haul a detainee before a judge and justify why they are being held.
cards.helpfulHint: Its second Latin word is the root of 'corpse' and 'corporal.'

cards.prompt: Under the 1967 Outer Space Treaty signed by over a hundred nations, no government on Earth may legally claim what?
cards.funFactWhy: Even planting the American flag on the Sea of Tranquility in 1969 was purely ceremonial — Article II explicitly forbids turning the Moon into anyone's sovereign real estate.
cards.helpfulHint: Those novelty websites selling acres of lunar craters are strictly for laughs under Article II.
choices: Orbital radio frequencies allocated by treaty
Jurisdiction over astronauts inside their own capsule
Sovereign ownership of the Moon or any planet

cards.prompt: When a U.S. president leaves a bill unsigned and Congress adjourns within ten days (excluding Sundays), the bill dies via what wardrobe-inspired maneuver?
cards.funFactWhy: Unlike a regular veto, Congress cannot override this silent rejection — presidents simply let the legislative clock run out as though stuffing the bill into a jacket.
cards.helpfulHint: Think of the small sewn pouch inside a suit coat where an executive might quietly stash an unwanted parchment.

cards.prompt: When twelve nations signed the 1959 Antarctic Treaty, what clever legal compromise did they strike over overlapping territorial claims to the South Pole?
cards.funFactWhy: Seven countries still draw pie-slice maps of Antarctica — three of which overlap on the Antarctic Peninsula — yet everyone politely agrees to disagree while sharing science stations.
cards.helpfulHint: Appropriate for Earth's coldest continent, Article IV kept every existing claim on ice while banning any fresh land grabs.
choices: Auctioned disputed sectors through the World Bank every 50 years
Awarded each pie slice to whichever state built the largest airfield
Transferred full sovereignty directly to the United Nations Secretariat
Froze existing claims in abeyance while barring any new ones

cards.prompt: Prime patrol: select the THREE genuine prime numbers hiding among three famously deceptive composite imposters.

cards.prompt: Three of these famous mathematical numbers are genuinely irrational — spot the ONE rational imposter disguised in the lineup.

cards.prompt: Select the THREE Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems that still stand unsolved with a $1 million bounty waiting.

cards.prompt: Dial in the exact sum of the four interior angles inside any flat four-sided polygon — from a neat rectangle to a wild kite.

cards.prompt: In the famous Birthday Paradox, how few people need to gather in one room before there is better than a 50% chance that two of them share the exact same birthday?

cards.prompt: Across all 43 quintillion scrambles of a standard 3x3 Rubik's Cube, what is the maximum number of face turns ('God's Number') ever required to solve it optimally?

cards.prompt: French author Georges Perec wrote his entire 300-page 1969 mystery novel "La Disparition" ("A Void")—and Gilbert Adair translated it into English—without using which single letter even once?
cards.funFactWhy: A book written while deliberately banning a letter is called a lipogram—and somehow Perec pulled off a gripping noir mystery without the most frequent letter in both French and English!
cards.helpfulHint: It is the most common letter in the English alphabet—and oddly absent from this very hint’s final word: "skip." Wait—check the letter after D!

cards.prompt: Who flew too close to the Sun?

cards.prompt: Tap all 3 famous mystery novels written by Agatha Christie—ignore the 3 rival crime classics!

cards.prompt: George Orwell finished typing "Nineteen Eighty-Four" on a remote Scottish island by flipping the last two digits of what publication year?

cards.helpfulHint: He wrote it in 1948, and publishers put it on bookshelves the very next summer.

cards.prompt: In Dante Alighieri’s "Inferno," how many concentric circles of Hell must Dante and Virgil descend through?
cards.funFactWhy: Dante built the entire Divine Comedy around the number three and its square: 3 canticles, 3-line terza rima stanzas, 33 cantos each (plus 1 intro = 100), and 9 concentric circles of Hell.
cards.helpfulHint: Think three times three—a tidy single-digit square number.

cards.prompt: Name the iconic 1897 epistolary novel revealed across these three escalating clues.

cards.prompt: A fair coin has just landed Heads five times in a row. What is the exact probability that the sixth flip lands Tails?
cards.funFactWhy: Coins have zero memory! Believing a streak makes the opposite outcome "overdue" is the Gambler’s Fallacy—infamously displayed at a Monte Carlo roulette wheel in 1913 when black hit 26 times straight and bettors lost millions.
cards.helpfulHint: Ignore the first five flips completely—the coin has no idea what happened five seconds ago.

cards.prompt: In mathematics, what does 0! (zero factorial) equal?
cards.funFactWhy: There is exactly one way to arrange zero objects in a line (doing nothing at all!), and defining 0! = 1 keeps every combinatorics formula and power series working smoothly.

cards.prompt: Three of these odd numbers are true primes—spot the 1 composite imposter wearing a prime disguise!

cards.prompt: On a flat Euclidean plane, what do the three interior angles of ANY triangle always add up to (in degrees)?
cards.funFactWhy: On a flat sheet of paper it is always 180 degrees—yet draw a giant triangle on Earth’s curved globe from the North Pole to two Equator spots and you can easily build a triangle with three 90-degree corners (270 degrees)!
cards.helpfulHint: Exactly half of a full 360-degree spin.

cards.prompt: Excluding Jokers, how many cards are in a standard Anglo-American playing deck (and how many weeks fill a calendar year)?
cards.funFactWhy: Because 52! (52 factorial) equals roughly 8 followed by 67 zeroes, every time you thoroughly shuffle a standard deck of cards, you almost certainly create an exact order that has never existed before in human history.
